title: Comment on "Topography of Fermi arcs in t-PtBi$_2$ using high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy" arXiv:2503.08841 (cond-mat)
abstract: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and scanning tunneling spectroscopy have established surface superconductivity in the Weyl semimetal t-PtBi$_2$, whereas O'Leary et al. concluded from an independent ARPES experiment that superconducting signatures are absent above 3 K. Here we reanalyze the complete deposited data of O'Leary et al. Using only experimentally determined momentum-distribution-curve (MDC) maxima, energy-distribution-curve (EDC) peak positions, and leading edges, we find a strongly anisotropic low-energy gap and dispersion back-bending that closely reproduce the magnitude and angular dependence reported independently by Changdar et al. We further show that the temperature-dependent data of Ref.~\cite{Oleary} originate from the other surface termination and were presented using temperature-dependent energy translations, momentum translations, and momentum rescalings. Registering the original temperature-dependent datasets using the metallic bulk Fermi cutoff reveals finite gaps of approximately 2, 2, 1, and 0.8 meV at the four Fermi crossings. Thus the independently acquired data of O'Leary et al., obtained on different samples and with a different photon energy, confirm rather than contradict the previously reported anisotropic superconducting gap and additionally show that an anisotropic low-energy suppression persists to 19 K.
summary: This work re-examines ARPES data on the Weyl semimetal t-PtBi2 to resolve conflicting reports on its superconducting state. By reanalyzing raw data using robust spectral features, the authors confirm the existence of a persistent, anisotropic superconducting gap up to 19 K. The study emphasizes the critical importance of consistent data registration when comparing temperature-dependent measurements in condensed matter spectroscopy.
main_problem: The paper re-evaluates conflicting experimental claims regarding the presence and nature of superconductivity in the Weyl semimetal t-PtBi2, specifically challenging the assertion that superconducting signatures vanish above 3 K.
main_result: The reanalysis of independent ARPES data confirms a strongly anisotropic low-energy superconducting gap and persistent low-energy suppression up to 19 K, contradicting previous interpretations that suggested the gap disappears at low temperatures.
method: The authors reanalyzed deposited ARPES data using only robust spectral features (MDC maxima, EDC peak positions, leading edges) rather than relying on full spectral modeling or potentially flawed temperature-dependent data processing.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the Weyl semimetal material t-PtBi2, a system known for its topological electronic properties and exhibiting surface superconductivity.
key_observables: Anisotropic low-energy superconducting gap magnitude ($\Delta$), dispersion back-bending, and the persistence of low-energy suppression across different temperatures (3 K to 19 K).
important_parameters: Gap values of approximately 2, 2, 1, and 0.8 meV at four Fermi crossings; temperatures up to 19 K.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that spectral features like leading edges and peak positions are reliable indicators of the superconducting gap, and that the bulk Fermi cutoff provides a consistent energy reference for relative measurements.
figures_summary: Figures show Fermi-surface maps illustrating gap anisotropy, raw EDC sequences demonstrating dispersion back-bending, and plots detailing the temperature evolution of the gap derived from reanalyzed datasets.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the conflict regarding superconductivity in t-PtBi2. It then details the rigorous reanalysis of O'Leary et al.'s data, confirming the anisotropic gap. Finally, it addresses the temperature dependence by showing that previous interpretations relied on flawed data registration techniques, concluding that the gap persists to higher temperatures.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the rigorous analysis of spectral features and the need for careful data registration in ARPES are crucial techniques applicable to any strongly correlated system where subtle energy scales are measured.
